title: Update: Identities Released And Possible Cause Named In Connection With Deadly Fire In Palermo - NewsBreak
text:
By Cori ,
1 days ago
Authorities have a better idea of what may have caused a deadly fire on the Leeman Arm Road in Palermo that killed one person and sent another to the hospital with severe injuries.
Read More: Investigation Underway After Serious Fire In Palermo, Maine
The fire broke out around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. When firefighters arrived on the scene, they found a badly burned adult male, who informed them that there was still someone inside the home. The injured man was LifeFlighted to Maine Medical Center for his injuries, where authorities say his condition is critical.
Download the WWMJ Mobile App Now According to Maine’s Department of Public Safety, several members of the State Fire Marshal’s Office spent the afternoon on the scene in Palermo on Tuesday. They located the remains of the second individual who was unaccounted for at the time of the fire. The body was sent to Augusta to be identified, and so the Medical Examiner’s office can determine how the person died.
Authorities believe the fire was initially started as a result of an explosion.
“Investigators believe there may have been an explosion inside the residence before the fire. The home was supplied with propane gas for appliances and heating. State Propane Inspectors assisted Investigators at the scene, and the cause of the explosion remains under investigation.”
While they are still waiting on a positive ID from the Chief Medical Examiner, authorities believe the remains they discovered inside the home, after the fire, belonged to 64-year-old Gary Crane Sr. His son is the man they found badly burned outside of the home and had to be LifeFlighted to Portland.
“His son, 45-year-old Gary Crane remains in critical condition at Maine Medical Center in Portland.”
They say the investigation is still ongoing.
Read More: Investigating A Tragic House Fire In Cambridge, Maine
Just last month, a home on Lakeview Drive in Oakland was destroyed due to an explosion , and 66-year-old Cliff Hannon had to be LifeFlighted to Maine Medical Center in Portland due to his injuries.

Read below to find out how you can proactively prepare for cold weather, with a little comedy. Jeshoots via Unsplash Stay Informed Stay Informed: The Governor’s Energy Office tracks heating fuel prices to help consumers make informed energy decisions. Media Lab Tune-Up! Make sure to schedule your yearly maintenance on your heating system to secure the system is operating properly and efficiently. Media Lab Energy Efficiency Weatherizing your house is extremely imporant. Keeping your home energy efficient will benefit you the entire season. Make sure to install a high efficiency heat pump which can help you save money this winter and use less fuel. Learn more about incentives & get energy saving tips from EfficiencyMaine.com and MaineHousing.com! Kostiantyn via Unsplash Lock Your Prices! Find out from your fuel provider about locking in a price for the entire heating season. This will assist you as security against unexpected price hikes. Alwways read contracts closely and ask questions to understand all details before you sign! Jupiterimages via Media Lab Set Thermostat to 68 Degrees According to a blog on Gassouth.com, for every degree you lower your thermostat below 70, you’ll save an easy 5% on your heating costs. Just a 2-degree decrease, from 70 to 68 degrees, rounds up to a nice 10% cut in your energy expenses. Inside Weather via Unsplash Move Furniture! Moving your couch, table, chairs, or furniture away from vents will help the air spread evenly into the room and not become trapped. Markus Spiske via Unsplash Wood Heater If you use wood to heat your home, read your firewood guide prepared by the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. Toa Heftiba via Unsplash Open Blinds Let the sun shine through your windows during the day for added warmth into the rooms in your house and at night close them so you don't lose heat through the windows. Media Lab Read your Propane Guide! If you heat with propane, make sure to read the Propane Consumer Guide (PDF), it will help you with pricing information on the best price for you, changing suppliers and potential start-up fees. Media Lab Set up Automatic Delivery! Inquire with your fuel provider about an automatic delivery.They will be able to observe your fuel usage, so you won’t run out of fuel. Automatic delivery also offers added security in the unlikely event of supply disruptions or very cold/inclement weather. This is When Mainers Decide it's Time to Turn on the Heat! Gallery Credit: Meghan Morrison Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva Unsplash / Canva The ABC's of Fire Safety 26 Tips to help keep your home and family safe, including what to do in case of a fire. Gallery Credit: Cindy Campbell Thinkstock, Getty Stock/ThinkStock A is for Ashes All those ashes need to be disposed of properly but, too often, are not. Ashes should be put into a metal container with a tight lid and then placed away from any structures. They should never be stored in cardboard (flammable) boxes or left uncovered, so the wind could scatter them and start a fire. WebSubstance, ThinkStock B is for Bedrooms Bedrooms should always be guarded by smoke detectors. Fire officials I've interviewed tell me that there should be detectors outside each sleeping area, one for the first floor, one for the second floor, etc. And, speaking of bedrooms, it's best to sleep with your door closed, so it creates a 'break' for the smoke and fire. Alarms going off? Touch that door before opening it. If it's hot, see if there's another way out. Photo by allison christine on Unsplash C is for Candles So many fires are started by candles that are placed too close to curtains or get knocked over by pets. Be careful where you place candles and make sure they're extinguished before going to bed or leaving the house. If you use them during power outages, consider buying battery-powered lanterns instead. rclassenlayouts, ThinkStock D is for Detectors The best defense in a fire is a smoke detector. It will wake you when you're sleeping, alert you to a fire in another part of the house, and give you time to get to safety. Place them in key areas, like the living room, outside sleeping areas, and in stairwells, and make sure you have them on all floors of the home. Questions about where they should be located? Contact your local fire department. Swillklitch, Getty Stock/ThinkStock E is for Exits E can actually stand for both exits and escape. Make sure everyone in your family knows where all the exits are, and we're not just talking about doors. Find two ways out of every room (door or window, for instance) and develop an escape plan. Your family should go over it frequently and even practice so, if fire breaks out, everyone knows which exit to use as an escape. wernerimages, ThinkStock F is for Firemen Most kids think firefighters are pretty cool. But put that same person in their firefighting gear in a house filled with smoke, and they could look pretty scary. So make sure your children know that, in the case of a fire, the firefighter is their friend and they should always follow their directions. Consider arranging with local firefighters for your kids to tour the fire station and get a demonstration of the gear, so they know what to expect. Vitaliy Halenov, ThinkStock G is for Generator Generators are lifesavers in a winter power outage, keeping the lights and the heat running. But, if they're not hooked up right, they could also cause a fire. Work with an electrician to get your portable generator hooked up, according to factory specifications. And allow the generator to cool down before refilling with gasoline. LSOphoto, ThinkStock H is for Heaters Many fires start with heating systems, so make a point of getting your furnace cleaned and serviced every year. Chimneys also need to be cleaned on a regular basis because a build up of creosote can start a chimney fire. And if your heat system begins acting up, call in an expert to see what's going on. Pixsooz, ThinkStock I is for Inspection If you have questions about how fire-safe your home is, contact your local fire department. Most will do a walk-through inspection and give you pointers about things you can change, like the locations of your smoke detectors. aleksandr yakovlev, ThinkStock J is for Just Get Out Have you played that game where you think about what you'd grab if your house caught fire? Photo albums or a treasured memento, perhaps? It's entertaining to think about but, if your house actually does catch fire, just get out. The most important 'item' you can save from a fire is yourself. If you have things you truly don't want to lose, consider putting them in a fire-proof box, but don't risk your life trying to salvage stuff. Halfpoint, ThinkStock K is for Kids Kids need as much knowledge as possible about how to behave in a fire, which exits to use, and even how to call 911. Again, make sure they understand that firefighters are there to save them and not to be afraid. Most fire departments will hold some sort of open house for families, so the kids can meet the people and see the equipment up close. Jasmina81, Getty Stock/ThinkStock L - Let the Firefighters Know Everyone's Safe Saving time can be a matter of life and death in a fire. So, if your house is burning, communicate with firefighters and let them know when everyone is out safely. Not spending time searching for family members who are already out of the fire could mean they get the fire out faster. Purestock, Getty Stock/ThinkStock M is for Meeting Place In order to know if everyone has made it out of a fire safely, designate a meeting place, away from any structures. You could tell everyone to meet by the tire swing in the big tree or in the next door neighbor's driveway. If everyone knows, and someone doesn't show up, it's time to tell the firefighters that someone didn't get out. Animaflora, ThinkStock N - Never Run Back Into a Burning Building Any firefighter will tell you to never, ever run back into a burning building. If you're out, stay out. Let the firefighters do their work. They have equipment that will protect them and allow them to see through the smoke. You don't. Too may lives are lost because people ran back into a burning house after making it out safely. tab1962, ThinkStock O is for Outlets Power strips are great, as long as you don't over load the outlet. But plugging too many things into one outlet can cause problems. So instead of plugging your big screen TV, stereo, phone chargers, and lamps into one outlet, consider running an extension cord to another one. fizkes, ThinkStock P is for Plan Every household should have an escape plan and each family member should know it well. The plan should include two exits from every room and the designated place to meet up, outside your home. If you have children, consider drawing it up and putting it on your fridge. If the kids see it everyday, they're more likely to remember. And every once in a while, do a practice run. The kids don't actually have to climb out the windows. Just make sure they know when it's the quickest way out. Motortion, Thinkstock Q is for Quickly Move to the Exit In case of fire, walk quickly but don't run to the nearest way out of the building. In a smoke-filled house, you can't see anything. And even though you think you know your home, battling smoke and fear will cause you to become disoriented very quickly. The last thing you need is to injure yourself before you can get to safety. Aaron Savage, Townsquare Media R is for Replace Batteries in Smoke Detectors We hear it every year. When you set your clocks ahead or back for daylight savings time, change the batteries in your smoke detectors. It's excellent advice. Not only will it ensure that your detectors are working properly, it will save you from that annoying 'beep beep' that sounds when the batteries are dying. MarianVejcik, ThinkStock S is for Stove Imagine you forget to turn a burner off. (and who hasn't done that?) Without realizing the burner is on, you place something flammable too close to it, like a paper plate or a towel. Next thing you know, you have a fire. Always double-check to make sure the stove and oven are turned off when you're done using them. And if you have a grease fire, don't ever run through the house with the flaming pan. That just spreads the fire. Cover it tightly with a lid and use baking soda or an extinguisher to put it out. noblige, ThinkStock T is for Teach Fire Safety to Your Children It's not enough to protect your children in case of fire, but is also imperative to teach them fire safety. Matches aren't toys. Never play with lighters. Stay away from the woodstove and fireplace. Don't light sticks in the outdoor firepit and then run around with them. These are just a few of the things kids need to understand, in order to protect themselves and your home in the future. Staras, ThinkStock U - Use Fireplace Screens and Barriers Fireplace screens aren't just decorative. They also keep the fire contained to the hearth and prevent hot embers from popping out of the hearth and onto your furniture. They are also effective at keeping children and pets from getting too close. Of course, it's also important to never hang things like wet socks on that screen to dry. Wimage72, Getty Stock/ThinkStock V is for Verify That Your Cigarette is Extinguished This is another of the top causes of house fires. Cigarettes. So keep ashtrays around the house and use them, making sure the cigarette is fully extinguished when you're done. Ashtrays should be emptied often, but only when you know nothing is still hot or burning. And place them in areas where they're not apt to get knocked over by kids or pets. Masaki Matsuba, Getty Images/iStockphoto W is for Woodstove Woodstoves are a great heat source and they smell so good. But they can also be dangerous unless used wisely. So keep combustibles far away from the woodstove and keep the door shut unless you're adding more wood. The stovepipe should be cleaned on a regular basis, to prevent creosote buildup. And teach your children to stay away and not to touch it. artisteer, ThinkStock X is for Extinguisher (okay, we cheated a little) Every home should have at least one fire extinguisher because not every fire is going to devastate your house. That is, if you're prepared. Educate everyone in the family about how to use the extinguishers and keep track of when they need to be recharged. It could mean the difference between a small kitchen fire and losing everything when it gets out of control. TeoLazarev, Getty Stock/ThinkStock Y is Yell for Help What do you do if you're trapped in a burning house? Yell. Loud. If you can call 911, do it. But then start yelling, so neighbors, firefighters, and/or passersby know that someone is trapped in the fire. Brett Bojduj, ThinkStock Z is for Zippo (or any) Lighters We're not picking on Zippo lighters, but since it starts with Z, it fit. Too many fires are started by kids playing with matches or lighters so keep them out of reach, as much as possible and educate the kids on the dangers of using them. Lighters are bright and colorful and fun to flick. Children need to understand they're not toys.
